q: An object falling through a fluid reaches its terminal velocity when:
o: The net force on it becomes zero
The drag force becomes greater than its weight
Its acceleration becomes equal to g
x: At terminal velocity the upward forces (drag, plus upthrust) balance the weight, so the net force and acceleration are zero and the speed stays constant. For a body falling from rest the drag never exceeds the weight.

q: According to Stokes' law, the drag force on a small sphere of radius r moving with speed v through a fluid of viscosity η is:
x: Stokes' law is F = 6πηrv: drag is directly proportional to radius, speed and viscosity. It holds for small spheres moving slowly, in laminar flow.

q: A raindrop starts falling from rest through still air. Which describes its acceleration as it falls?
o: It stays equal to g throughout
It decreases from g to zero
It increases from zero to g
It decreases from g to a constant non-zero value
x: At the start the speed, and so the drag, is zero, so the acceleration is g. As the speed rises the drag grows, the net force falls, and the acceleration falls to zero at terminal velocity.

q: Ignoring upthrust, the terminal velocity of a small sphere is v_t = 2ρgr²/9η. A sphere of the same material but twice the radius has a terminal velocity that is:
x: v_t is proportional to r², so doubling r multiplies v_t by 2² = 4. The weight grows eight times (∝ r³), but the drag also grows with r.

q: A small sphere of radius 1 × 10⁻³ m moves at a steady 0.02 m s⁻¹ through oil of viscosity 0.5 Pa s. Using Stokes' law, the drag force on it is:
A steel ball reaches terminal velocity in glycerine. In a liquid of the same density but twice the viscosity, its terminal velocity (using Stokes' law) would be:
x: At terminal velocity the drag 6πηrv equals the weight minus the upthrust, which is unchanged. So ηv stays constant: doubling η halves v.

q: Two raindrops have radii in the ratio 1 : 3. Assuming Stokes' law applies and ignoring upthrust, the ratio of their terminal velocities is:
x: Weight ∝ r³ while drag ∝ rv, so mg = 6πηrv gives v ∝ r². The ratio is 1² : 3² = 1 : 9.

q: A small ball is dropped into a tall jar of oil. On its velocity–time graph, once terminal velocity is reached, the graph:
o: Becomes a straight line with slope g
Becomes a horizontal line with zero slope
x: The slope of a v–t graph is the acceleration. At terminal velocity the acceleration is zero, so the graph levels off into a horizontal line.

q: A small sphere falls at terminal velocity through a liquid. Which balance of forces is correct?
x: Weight acts downward; drag (opposing the downward motion) and upthrust both act upward. At terminal velocity the net force is zero, so weight = drag + upthrust.

q: A tiny water droplet of radius 3 × 10⁻⁵ m falls through air of viscosity 2 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s. Using v_t = 2ρgr²/9η with ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 10 m s⁻² (ignore upthrust), its terminal velocity is:
Fluid drag is:
o: A resistive force that opposes the motion of a body through a fluid
The upward force on a body due to the fluid it displaces
The pressure exerted by a fluid at rest
The attraction between molecules at a liquid surface
x: Drag is the retarding (frictional) force a fluid exerts on a body moving through it, acting opposite to the body's motion relative to the fluid. The upward force from displaced fluid is upthrust.

q: According to Stokes' law, the drag force on a small sphere moving through a fluid does NOT depend on:
x: F = 6πηrv contains only η, r and v. The sphere's density affects its weight and so its terminal velocity, but not the drag at a given speed.

q: From Stokes' law, the SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity η is:
x: η = F/(6πrv), so its unit is N / (m × m s⁻¹) = N s m⁻², which equals Pa s or kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹.

q: The dimensions of the coefficient of viscosity are:
x: η = F/(rv) has dimensions [MLT⁻²] / ([L][LT⁻¹]) = [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]. [ML⁻¹T⁻²] is the dimension of pressure.

q: A small sphere moves slowly through a viscous liquid so that Stokes' law applies. If its speed is doubled, the drag force on it:
x: In Stokes' law F = 6πηrv the drag is directly proportional to the speed, so doubling v doubles F.

q: A small ball is thrown vertically upward through still air. While it is moving upward, the air drag on it acts:
o: Upward, in the direction of motion
Nowhere, since drag acts only on falling bodies
x: Drag always opposes the motion of a body relative to the fluid. On the way up it acts downward, adding to the weight; on the way down it acts upward.

q: Fish, birds and racing cars have streamlined shapes mainly so that:
o: The upthrust on them is increased
The fluid drag on them is reduced
The viscosity of the surrounding fluid is reduced
x: A streamlined shape lets the fluid flow smoothly round the body with less turbulence, which reduces drag. Shape does not change the weight or the fluid's viscosity.

q: For a small sphere moving through a viscous fluid (Stokes' law), the radius is halved and the speed is doubled. The drag force:
x: F ∝ rv, so the new force ∝ (r/2)(2v) = rv: there is no change.

q: A marble is pulled at the same steady speed first through water and then through honey. The drag is greater in honey because honey has:
x: Drag is proportional to the viscosity η in Stokes' law. Honey's much larger internal friction between layers gives a much larger drag at the same speed.

q: A sphere of radius 5 × 10⁻³ m moving at 0.1 m s⁻¹ through a liquid experiences a drag of 3π × 10⁻⁴ N. Using Stokes' law, the viscosity of the liquid is:
Steady (streamline) flow of a fluid means that:
o: The velocity of the fluid at any given point does not change with time
The fluid moves with the same speed everywhere
The fluid particles move in circles
x: In steady flow every particle that passes a given point has the same velocity there as those before it. The speed may still differ from one point to another.

q: An ideal fluid is said to be incompressible. This means that:
o: Its velocity stays constant throughout the flow
Its density stays constant throughout the flow
Its pressure is the same everywhere
x: Incompressible means its volume, and so its density, does not change with pressure. Zero viscosity is the separate non-viscous condition.

q: Non-viscous flow of an ideal fluid means that:
o: The flow speed is the same at every point
There is no internal friction between adjacent layers of the fluid
x: Viscosity is internal friction between layers; a non-viscous fluid has none, so no energy is lost to friction as it flows. Incompressibility is a different property.

q: In steady flow, two streamlines can never cross each other because:
o: The fluid would become compressed at that point
At the crossing point a fluid particle would have two directions of velocity
The viscosity would become infinite there
The pressure would become zero there
x: The tangent to a streamline gives the direction of the velocity. If two streamlines crossed, a particle at that point would have two velocities at once, which is impossible.

q: In laminar flow:
o: Layers of fluid slide smoothly past one another
The fluid moves in irregular whirls and eddies
The fluid particles move randomly in all directions
The velocity at a point changes erratically
x: Laminar (streamline) flow is smooth and orderly: adjacent layers slide past each other without mixing. Eddies and erratic changes describe turbulent flow.

q: Which of the following is NOT an assumption about an ideal fluid?
o: There is strong internal friction between its layers
x: An ideal fluid is taken as steady, incompressible and non-viscous, so it has no internal friction. Strong internal friction describes a highly viscous real fluid.

q: In a streamline diagram of an ideal fluid in a pipe, the streamlines are drawn closer together in one region. In that region the fluid:
x: Crowded streamlines mean a smaller cross-section for the same flow, so by continuity the fluid moves faster there. An ideal (incompressible) fluid has the same density everywhere.

q: The tangent drawn at any point on a streamline gives:
o: The direction of the pipe's cross-sectional area
The direction of the fluid's velocity at that point
The direction perpendicular to the fluid's velocity
The direction of the weight of the fluid
x: A streamline is the path followed by fluid particles in steady flow, so its tangent at any point shows the direction of the velocity there.

q: Water flows steadily through a pipe that narrows. A water particle moving along a streamline:
o: Keeps the same speed at all points
Has a velocity that changes randomly at each point
Slows down as it enters the narrow part
Speeds up as it enters the narrow part, although the velocity at each fixed point stays constant in time
x: Steady flow does not mean the same speed all along the path: the particle speeds up in the narrow part, but every particle reaching a given point has the same velocity there. Slowing down would break continuity.

q: A liquid keeps the same density under any pressure and the velocity at each point never changes, but adjacent layers exert friction on one another. Which ideal-fluid condition does it NOT satisfy?
x: Friction between layers means the liquid is viscous, so it fails the non-viscous condition. Constant density makes it incompressible, and an unchanging velocity at each point makes the flow steady (streamline).

q: Turbulent flow of a fluid is characterised by:
o: Smooth layers sliding past one another
Irregular motion with eddies and whirlpools
A velocity at each point that never changes
x: In turbulent flow the motion is irregular, with eddies (small whirlpools), and the velocity at a point keeps changing. The other descriptions fit laminar flow.

q: The flow of a viscous fluid changes from laminar to turbulent when:
o: Its speed falls below a certain value
Its speed exceeds a certain critical value
x: At low speeds viscous flow is laminar; above a critical speed the smooth layers break up into eddies and the flow becomes turbulent. Higher viscosity tends to keep flow laminar.

q: Smoke rising from an incense stick goes up as a smooth thread at first but breaks into irregular swirls a little higher up. This is because:
o: The smoke speeds up as it rises until the flow becomes turbulent
The smoke slows down as it rises and becomes laminar
The viscosity of air increases with height
The smoke particles become heavier as they rise
x: The hot smoke accelerates upward. Once its speed passes the critical value, laminar flow changes to turbulent flow, seen as swirls and eddies.

q: In turbulent flow, the velocity of the fluid at a fixed point:
o: Is the same as at every other point
x: Turbulent flow is unsteady: eddies pass through any fixed point, so the velocity there keeps changing in size and direction.

q: When a tap is opened slightly, water comes out as a smooth, clear column; when it is opened fully, the stream becomes rough and broken. This change happens because:
o: The water becomes more viscous at high speed
The water is compressed at high speed
The flow speed drops when the tap is fully open
The higher flow speed makes the flow turbulent
x: Opening the tap fully raises the flow speed above the critical value, so the smooth laminar column becomes turbulent. Water stays practically incompressible.

q: Stokes' law, F = 6πηrv, does not apply to a sphere moving at high speed through a fluid because:
o: The flow around the sphere becomes turbulent
The viscosity of the fluid becomes zero
x: Stokes' law is derived for slow, laminar flow around a small sphere. At high speeds the flow becomes turbulent and the drag no longer follows F = 6πηrv.

q: Compared with laminar flow, turbulent flow of a fluid through a pipe:
o: Wastes less energy, because the fluid moves faster
Has no internal friction at all
Wastes more energy, because eddies convert kinetic energy into internal energy
x: Eddies in turbulent flow dissipate kinetic energy into internal (heat) energy, so more energy is lost and resistance is greater than in laminar flow.

q: Water flows smoothly (laminar) through a pipe. Which change would make the flow more likely to become turbulent?
o: Making the inner wall of the pipe smoother
x: Laminar flow breaks down into turbulence when the speed rises above a critical value. Lower speed and higher viscosity both help keep the flow laminar, and smoother walls disturb it less.

q: Bernoulli's equation and streamline diagrams cannot be applied exactly to turbulent flow because:
o: The flow is not steady, so the velocity at a point keeps changing
The pressure becomes the same everywhere
The fluid stops moving inside the eddies
x: Bernoulli's equation assumes steady, streamline flow. In turbulent flow the velocity at a point changes erratically, so there are no fixed streamlines (and energy is also lost in eddies).

q: Most fluid flows met in everyday life, such as rivers, wind and the air flow around moving vehicles, are:
x: Laminar flow occurs only at low speeds. Most practical flows are fast enough to be turbulent.

q: Which of the following flows is turbulent?
o: Honey poured slowly from a spoon
Water rushing over rocks in a fast mountain stream
A thin layer of oil creeping down a glass plate
x: Fast flow over obstacles produces eddies, which is turbulence. The other three are slow, viscous flows that stay laminar.

q: Stokes' law cannot be used to find the air drag on a car moving at 30 m s⁻¹ because:
o: The car's speed is too low
The air flow around the car is turbulent and the car is not a small sphere
x: Stokes' law applies only to small spheres in slow, laminar flow. A car at motorway speed leaves a turbulent wake, so its drag must be found in other ways.

q: Competitive swimmers wear smooth, tight swimsuits and caps. The main reason is to:
o: Increase the viscosity of the water
Reduce turbulent drag in the water
Increase the drag so they can push off it
x: Smooth surfaces reduce the turbulence of the water flowing past the swimmer, so drag is reduced. They do not change upthrust or the water's viscosity.

q: Which statement about practical fluid flow is correct?
o: Most practical flows are laminar; turbulence is rare
Most practical flows are turbulent; laminar flow occurs mainly at low speeds
Turbulent flow occurs only in gases
Real fluids always behave as ideal fluids
x: Laminar flow needs low speeds; in practice most flows of water, air and other fluids are fast enough to be turbulent. Liquids as well as gases can be turbulent.

q: Results worked out for an ideal fluid are only approximate for real flows because real flows are:
x: The ideal model assumes non-viscous, steady (laminar) flow. Real fluids have viscosity and most practical flows are turbulent, so energy is lost and the simple equations hold only approximately.

q: Stokes' law (laminar drag) can be applied with good accuracy to which of the following?
o: A cricket ball moving at high speed through air
A car moving along a motorway
A tiny oil droplet drifting slowly down through still air
x: Stokes' law needs a small sphere moving slowly so that the flow round it stays laminar, which fits a tiny oil droplet. The other three are large bodies at high speeds in turbulent flow.

q: When a fast river flows past a bridge pillar, swirling eddies form behind the pillar. These eddies show that the flow there is:
x: Eddies and whirlpools are the mark of turbulent flow, which is common wherever fast-moving fluid passes obstacles.

q: Because most practical flows are turbulent rather than laminar, which of the following is true?
o: Drag on vehicles can always be found from Stokes' law
Real resistance to motion in fluids is usually greater than simple laminar formulas predict
Fluids flow through pipes without any energy loss
Bernoulli's equation applies exactly to real pipelines
x: Turbulent flow dissipates more energy than laminar flow, so real resistance and pressure losses exceed laminar predictions. Stokes' law and the ideal Bernoulli equation hold only approximately.

q: An ideal fluid flows through a pipe that narrows. According to the equation of continuity, in the narrow part the fluid's:
x: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so a smaller area means a greater speed. An incompressible fluid's density stays the same.

q: Water flows at 2 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of cross-sectional area 4 cm². The pipe narrows to an area of 1 cm². The speed of the water in the narrow part is:
x: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂: 4 × 2 = 1 × v₂, so v₂ = 8 m s⁻¹.

q: The diameter of a pipe carrying an ideal fluid is halved at a constriction. The speed of the fluid in the constriction becomes:
x: Area ∝ d², so halving the diameter makes the area one quarter. From Av = constant, the speed becomes four times as large.

q: Water flows at 3 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of cross-sectional area 2 × 10⁻³ m². The volume of water delivered per second is:
x: Volume flow rate = Av = 2 × 10⁻³ × 3 = 6 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹, which is 6 litres per second.

q: In the equation of continuity, the product Av (cross-sectional area × flow speed) has the SI unit:
x: m² × m s⁻¹ = m³ s⁻¹, the volume flow rate. kg s⁻¹ is the unit of the mass flow rate ρAv.

q: A hose of cross-sectional area 1 cm² delivers water at 2 m s⁻¹. How long does it take to fill a 12-litre bucket? (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³)
x: Flow rate = Av = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m² × 2 m s⁻¹ = 2 × 10⁻⁴ m³ s⁻¹ = 0.2 L s⁻¹. Time = 12 / 0.2 = 60 s.

q: A fatty deposit reduces the cross-sectional area of an artery to one third of its normal value. Treating blood as an ideal fluid, its speed through the narrowed part becomes:
o: One third of the normal speed
The same as the normal speed
x: From A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, reducing the area to one third makes the speed three times larger. Nine times would wrongly square the area ratio.

q: Blood leaves the aorta (area 3 cm²) at 30 cm s⁻¹ and later passes through the capillaries, whose total cross-sectional area is about 900 cm². The average blood speed in the capillaries is about:
x: Av = constant: 3 × 30 = 900 × v, so v = 90 / 900 = 0.1 cm s⁻¹. The speed is low because the total area of all the capillaries is huge, even though each one is tiny.

q: A main pipe of cross-sectional area 8 cm² carries water at speed v. It divides into two identical branch pipes, each of area 2 cm². The speed of the water in each branch is:
x: The flow is shared between the branches: 8v = 2 × 2 × v′, so v′ = 2v. Answering 4v forgets that the flow splits into two branches.

q: A smooth stream of water falling from a tap becomes narrower as it falls. This is because:
o: Its speed decreases, so its cross-sectional area decreases
Its speed increases, so by continuity its cross-sectional area decreases
The water is compressed by air pressure
Surface tension pulls the water back into the tap
x: Gravity speeds the water up as it falls. Since Av stays constant, the cross-section of the stream must shrink as v increases.

q: The equation of continuity is a statement of the law of conservation of:
x: It says the mass of fluid entering a section of pipe per second equals the mass leaving per second, since mass is neither created nor destroyed. Bernoulli's equation expresses conservation of energy.

q: The mass of fluid passing a cross-section of a pipe per second (the mass flow rate) is equal to:
x: In time Δt a volume AvΔt passes, of mass ρAvΔt. Dividing by Δt gives the mass flow rate ρAv.

q: The general form of the continuity equation is ρ₁A₁v₁ = ρ₂A₂v₂. It simplifies to A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ only when the fluid is:
x: For an incompressible fluid ρ₁ = ρ₂, so the density cancels. Viscosity does not appear in the continuity equation.

q: In steady flow through a pipe with no leaks, the mass of fluid entering one end per second equals the mass leaving the other end per second because:
o: The pressure is the same at both ends
The speed is the same at both ends
The pipe has the same cross-section everywhere
Fluid cannot pile up or disappear inside the pipe
x: With steady flow and no leaks, the mass inside the section stays constant, so mass in per second must equal mass out per second. This holds even when area, speed and pressure differ.

q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows at 5 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of cross-sectional area 2 × 10⁻⁴ m². The mass flow rate is:
x: Mass flow rate = ρAv = 1000 × 2 × 10⁻⁴ × 5 = 1 kg s⁻¹.

q: The SI unit of the quantity ρAv (density × area × speed) is:
x: kg m⁻³ × m² × m s⁻¹ = kg s⁻¹, the unit of mass flow rate. m³ s⁻¹ is the unit of Av alone.

q: A gas flows steadily through a pipe of uniform cross-section. Between two points its density falls to half its earlier value. By conservation of mass, its speed at the second point is:
x: ρ₁A₁v₁ = ρ₂A₂v₂ with equal areas gives ρv = constant, so halving ρ doubles v. Using A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ alone wrongly gives equal speeds, because a gas is compressible.

q: An incompressible fluid moves with speed v through a pipe of cross-sectional area S. The volume of fluid that passes a given cross-section in time t is:
x: In time t the fluid moves a distance vt, so a cylinder of volume S × vt passes the cross-section. Multiplying by density gives the mass, the basis of the continuity equation.

q: Water flows through a pipe with a mass flow rate of 2 kg s⁻¹. The pipe's cross-sectional area is 4 × 10⁻⁴ m² and the density of water is 1000 kg m⁻³. The speed of the water is:
According to Bernoulli's effect, in the horizontal flow of a fluid, where the speed of the fluid is higher the pressure is:
x: From P + ½ρv² = constant for horizontal flow, a larger v means a smaller P. This is Bernoulli's effect.

q: Plaque narrows a section of an artery. Applying Bernoulli's principle, what happens at the narrowed section?
o: Blood speeds up and its pressure drops, so the artery may partly collapse
Blood slows down and its pressure rises, so the artery bulges
Blood speeds up and its pressure rises
Blood flow stops completely and the pressure becomes zero
x: By continuity blood moves faster through the narrow part, and by Bernoulli's effect its pressure there falls. The greater outside pressure can then squeeze the artery, which may close briefly and flutter.

q: In measuring blood pressure with a sphygmomanometer, the cuff is inflated above systolic pressure and then slowly released. The first sound heard through the stethoscope marks the:
x: Once the cuff pressure falls just below the systolic (peak) pressure, blood spurts through the squeezed artery at each heartbeat and makes sounds. That cuff reading is the systolic pressure.

q: A healthy adult's blood pressure is written as 120/80 mmHg (torr). The value 120 is the:
o: Systolic pressure, when the heart contracts
Diastolic pressure, when the heart relaxes
Difference between arterial and venous pressure
x: The larger number is the systolic pressure, reached when the heart contracts and pumps blood. The smaller number, 80, is the diastolic pressure, when the heart relaxes.

q: The sounds heard through a stethoscope during blood-pressure measurement are produced because the blood flow in the partly squeezed artery is:
x: When the cuff partly closes the artery, blood spurts through at high speed and the flow becomes turbulent, which is noisy. Smooth laminar flow is silent.

q: As the cuff pressure of a sphygmomanometer is lowered further, the sounds heard through the stethoscope suddenly stop. At this point:
o: The cuff pressure has risen above systolic pressure
The blood has stopped flowing in the artery
The cuff pressure has fallen below diastolic pressure and the flow becomes smooth (laminar)
x: Below diastolic pressure the artery stays open throughout the heartbeat, so the flow becomes laminar and silent. The cuff reading when the sounds stop is the diastolic pressure.

q: An aeroplane wing (aerofoil) is shaped so that air flows faster over its upper surface than under it. This produces lift because:
o: The pressure above the wing is higher than the pressure below it
The air above the wing is denser
The drag on the wing acts upward
The pressure above the wing is lower than the pressure below it
x: By Bernoulli's effect the faster air above the wing has lower pressure. The higher pressure below pushes the wing upward, giving lift.

q: A Venturi meter is used to:
o: Measure the speed (flow rate) of a fluid in a pipe from a pressure difference
Measure the viscosity of a liquid
Measure the density of a gas
Measure blood pressure directly inside an artery
x: A Venturi meter has a narrow throat in a pipe. The pressure difference between the wide part and the throat, used with Bernoulli's equation and continuity, gives the flow speed.

q: In a perfume spray (atomiser), squeezing the bulb sends a jet of air across the top of a tube dipping into the liquid. The liquid rises up the tube because:
o: The fast air raises the pressure at the top of the tube
The liquid is attracted by the moving air
The fast air lowers the pressure at the top of the tube, so the higher pressure on the liquid surface pushes it up
x: Fast-moving air has low pressure. Atmospheric pressure on the liquid in the bottle is then greater and forces the liquid up the tube, where the jet breaks it into droplets.

q: Blood pressure is normally measured on the upper arm, at about the level of the heart. The reason is that:
o: Blood flows fastest in the upper arm
Pressure in a fluid changes with height by ρgh, so readings at other levels would differ
Blood is incompressible only near the heart
The arm has no arteries below the elbow
x: From P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, pressure is greater at lower points and smaller at higher points. Measuring at heart level avoids this ρgh difference, so the reading matches the pressure at the heart.

q: For an ideal fluid flowing through a horizontal tube, Bernoulli's equation is:
x: For a horizontal tube the ρgh term is the same at both ends and drops out, leaving P + ½ρv² = constant.

q: In deriving Bernoulli's equation, fluid at the wide end (pressure P₁, area A₁) is pushed through a distance Δx₁. The work done on it by the pressure force is:
x: Force = pressure × area = P₁A₁, and work = force × distance = P₁A₁Δx₁. Since A₁Δx₁ is the volume V pushed in, this equals P₁V.

q: In the derivation of Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal tube, the net work done on a volume V of fluid by the pressure forces at the two ends equals:
o: The change in gravitational potential energy only
The change in kinetic energy, ½m(v₂² − v₁²)
Zero, because the tube is horizontal
x: Net work = (P₁ − P₂)V. In a horizontal tube there is no change in potential energy, and an ideal fluid has no viscosity, so all this work becomes the gain in kinetic energy.

q: Bernoulli's equation is an application of the principle of conservation of:
x: It comes from the work–energy principle: work done by pressure forces equals the gain in kinetic (and potential) energy. Conservation of mass gives the equation of continuity instead.

q: In Bernoulli's equation, the term ½ρv² has the same unit as:
x: kg m⁻³ × m² s⁻² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻² = N m⁻² = Pa. The term is kinetic energy per unit volume, which has the unit of pressure.

q: When Bernoulli's equation P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant is applied to a horizontal tube, the term ρgh can be dropped because:
o: Gravity does not act on a moving fluid
The speed is the same at both ends
Both ends are at the same height, so there is no change in potential energy
x: In a horizontal tube both ends are at the same height, so ρgh is equal on both sides and cancels. Gravity still acts but does no net work on the fluid.

q: Which assumption is NOT used in deriving Bernoulli's equation?
x: The derivation assumes an ideal fluid in steady, streamline flow: non-viscous (no energy lost to friction) and incompressible (the same volume enters and leaves). Turbulent flow breaks these assumptions.

q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows through a horizontal pipe. At one point its speed is 2 m s⁻¹ and the pressure is 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa. At a narrower point its speed is 4 m s⁻¹. The pressure there is:

In the derivation of Bernoulli's equation, the volume of fluid pushed in at the wide end in time Δt is taken as equal to the volume leaving the narrow end in the same time. This is justified because the fluid is:
o: Non-viscous, so no energy is lost
Moving at the same speed at both ends
Incompressible, so continuity gives A₁v₁Δt = A₂v₂Δt
x: For an incompressible fluid in steady flow, continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) means equal volumes pass both ends in the same time. Being non-viscous matters for the energy balance, not for equal volumes.

q: Which is the correct order of steps in deriving Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal tube?
o: Pressures at both ends equated → continuity applied → kinetic energy set to zero
Gain in potential energy found → equated to work done against viscosity → divide by mass
Divide by volume → work done by gravity found → equated to the change in pressure
Work done by pressure forces at both ends → net work equated to gain in kinetic energy → divide by volume to get P + ½ρv² = constant
x: The net work (P₁ − P₂)V done by the pressure forces equals ½m(v₂² − v₁²). Dividing by V (with m/V = ρ) and rearranging gives P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂².

q: Air is blown gently between two sheets of paper hanging parallel and close together. The sheets:
o: Swing together in the same direction
x: The fast-moving air between the sheets has lower pressure than the still air outside, so the outside air pushes the sheets together (Bernoulli's effect).

q: Two ships sailing side by side, close together and in the same direction, tend to be drawn towards each other. This is because:
o: Water between them is at rest, raising the pressure there
The ships attract each other strongly by gravity
Water flows faster between them, lowering the pressure there
x: Water squeezed between the hulls moves faster relative to them, so its pressure is lower than on the outer sides. The pressure difference pushes the ships together.

q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows at 1 m s⁻¹ in the wide section of a horizontal Venturi tube. The throat has one third of the wide section's area. The pressure difference between the wide section and the throat is:
x: Continuity: v₂ = 3 × 1 = 3 m s⁻¹. ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = ½ × 1000 × (9 − 1) = 4000 Pa.

q: During a strong windstorm, the roof of a house can be lifted off. According to Bernoulli's effect this happens because:
o: Fast wind over the roof lowers the pressure above it, so the higher pressure inside pushes it up
The wind increases the pressure above the roof
The still air inside the house has lower pressure than the air outside
The wind reduces the weight of the roof
x: Air rushing over the roof has low pressure, while the still air inside the house stays near atmospheric pressure. The upward pressure difference across the roof can lift it.

q: A person standing near the edge of a platform as a fast train passes feels pushed towards the train. This is because:
o: The air near the train is at higher pressure
The train attracts the person by gravity
Fast-moving air between the person and the train has lower pressure
The air behind the person moves faster
x: The train drags air along at high speed, and by Bernoulli's effect the pressure there falls. The higher pressure of the still air behind the person pushes them towards the train.

q: Wind blowing across the top of a chimney helps smoke rise up the chimney because:
o: The wind raises the pressure at the top, forcing smoke down
The wind cools the smoke, making it denser
The fast wind lowers the pressure at the top, so air and smoke are pushed up from below
The wind increases the viscosity of the smoke
x: Moving air over the chimney top has lower pressure than the still air in the room below, so the pressure difference drives the smoke upward and out.

q: Air flows over one face of a sheet while the air on the other face is still. Using P + ½ρv² = constant, if the air speed is doubled, the pressure difference across the sheet becomes:
x: With still air on one side, ΔP = ½ρv². Since ΔP ∝ v², doubling v makes the pressure difference four times as large.

q: Air (density 1.2 kg m⁻³) flows at 50 m s⁻¹ over the top of a wing and at 40 m s⁻¹ under it. If the wing area is 10 m², the lift force on the wing is:
x: ΔP = ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²) = 0.6 × (2500 − 1600) = 540 Pa. Lift = ΔP × area = 540 × 10 = 5400 N. Using (50 − 40)² wrongly gives 600 N.

q: A light ping-pong ball floats steadily in an upward jet of air from a hair dryer; if it drifts sideways it moves back into the jet. In the textbook (Bernoulli) explanation, this happens because:
o: The still air around the jet is at lower pressure than the jet
The fast-moving air in the jet is at lower pressure than the still air around it
The jet makes the ball lighter
The jet's turbulence attracts the ball like a magnet
x: Air in the jet moves fast and so has lower pressure. If the ball drifts out, the higher pressure of the still air outside pushes it back into the jet.

q: Water flows through a horizontal Venturi meter. If the flow rate is increased, the pressure difference between the wide section and the narrow throat:
x: ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²). A larger flow rate raises both speeds in the same ratio, so the difference of their squares grows and the pressure difference increases.
